overview: Great Zimbabwe was a stone-built center created by ancestors of the Shona. Its surviving walls preserve part of a larger settlement of homes, courtyards and monumental enclosures.

items.text: Builders fitted local granite slabs together without mortar. Successive courses stepped inward, giving the curving walls a stabilizing inward slope.
Eight surviving soapstone bird sculptures combine human and bird features. Their precise meaning remains uncertain; an association with royal authority is one interpretation.
Stone walls stood beside homes made from daga, a building material of earth, with thatched roofs. Painted surfaces and enclosed courtyards formed parts of the lived settlement.

Excavations recovered imported glass beads, ceramics from China and Persia, and coins from Kilwa. These objects place the inland settlement within long-distance exchange networks; they do not, by themselves, identify every trader or route.

Six soapstone birds came from the Hill Complex's Eastern Enclosure. Their setting supports interpretations involving ritual or royal authority, but their original arrangement and precise meaning remain uncertain.

sources.note: Brief synthesis, excavated trade objects; Authenticity, continuing spiritual use. Its categorical abandonment explanation requires comparison with recent scholarship.

sources.title: Chirikure, Pollard, Manyanga and Bandama, A Bayesian chronology for Great Zimbabwe (2013)
sources.note: Abstract and chronological discussion; occupation continued after the conventionally cited 1450 endpoint.

ending.text: Great Zimbabwe did not simply empty in 1450. A study combining radiocarbon dates, stratigraphy and imported objects places occupation at least into the sixteenth century and probably the seventeenth, after its main building peak in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. The chronology does not identify a single conquest or establish one cause for the loss of political prominence. The site remains a place of spiritual practice for contemporary communities; the decline of a capital did not mean the disappearance of its people.
